name: Proteins: Life's Building Blocks
notation_note: Proteins are sequence-defined heteropolymers of up to 20 different L-α-amino acid monomers joined by peptide bonds; there is no single repeat unit for the class as a whole (sequence is the whole point). Individual proteins (e.g. keratin, collagen) get their own entries where relevant.

historical_images.alt: A black-and-white photograph of a woman kneeling outdoors, scraping the flesh side of an animal hide staked to the ground with a bone tool.
historical_images.caption: Fleshing a hide by hand — a craft built entirely on collagen chemistry, practiced for millennia before anyone had a name for the molecule involved.
historical_images.author: Edward Sheriff Curtis (1868-1954)

historical_images.alt: A seated half-length lithograph portrait of a man with dark curly hair and long sideburns, one arm resting on the back of a chair, signed 'G.J. Mulder' beneath.
historical_images.caption: Gerardus Johannes Mulder, whose 1838 analysis of albumin and fibrin proposed the shared substance that Berzelius would name protein.
historical_images.author: Rijksmuseum

historical_images.alt: A hand-colored illustration of a long, high-windowed chemistry laboratory around 1840, crowded with students in coats and top hats working at benches lined with glassware and furnaces.
historical_images.caption: Justus von Liebig's laboratory at Giessen, around 1840 — the year his textbook made 'protein' central to the emerging science of nutrition.
historical_images.author: Wilhelm Trautschold (1815 – 1877)

historical_images.alt: A large, densely woven sheet spider web, beaded all over with fine water droplets, spread across green shrubbery.
historical_images.caption: A sheet-web spider's silk, another structural protein whose engineering — strong, light, and self-spun — modern materials science is still trying to match.
historical_images.author: Dominicus Johannes Bergsma

density.conditions: Soy-protein-based industrial plastic (Wypych 'PR' entry), 20 °C; density is otherwise highly protein-specific and not meaningful for the class generally.

synthesis.industrial_process_notes: Biologically synthesized by ribosomes translating mRNA (up to ~20 amino acids/second in prokaryotes) via peptide bond formation between the amino and carboxyl groups of successive amino acids. Short peptides can also be made industrially by chemical peptide synthesis, but this is inefficient beyond a few hundred residues. The term 'protein' was coined by Jöns Jacob Berzelius in 1838, building on Gerardus Johannes Mulder's elemental-composition work.

structure_morphology.crystal_structure: Hierarchical structure: primary (sequence) -> secondary (α-helix/β-sheet, hydrogen-bond stabilized) -> tertiary (3-D fold, stabilized by hydrophobic core, salt bridges, disulfide bonds) -> quaternary (multi-chain assemblies).
structure_morphology.chain_flexibility_notes: Folding behavior and flexibility vary enormously by sequence; no single description applies across the class.

mw.conditions: Processed soy-protein-based material (Wypych 'PR' entry). Individual proteins vary enormously: raw soy protein 30,000-1,000,000, casein 19,000-25,200, albumins 10,000-15,000, globulins 150,000-450,000.

tg.conditions: Specific to individual proteins, not a general class value: wheat glutenin 181 °C, collagen 192 °C, gelatin 217 °C, elastin 252 °C.

tensile_modulus.conditions: Soy-protein-based industrial material (Wypych 'PR' entry, Young's modulus). Mechanical properties are otherwise specific to individual structural proteins (e.g. keratin, collagen, silk fibroin), not meaningful for 'proteins' as a class.

tensile_strength_at_break.conditions: Soy protein (as processed, Wypych 'PR' entry); drawn soy protein (2.5 draw ratio) reaches 99 MPa, zein 12.7 MPa (5-6 MPa cast).

elongation_at_break.conditions: Soy protein (Wypych 'PR' entry); zein reported much higher, 61-122%.

acids.conditions: Soy protein-based industrial material (Wypych 'PR' entry), dilute and concentrated.

hydrolysis_resistance.conditions: Peptide bonds are hydrolyzable (this is how digestion works) but rate depends heavily on structure/sequence.

processing_temp_range.conditions: Soy protein-based industrial material (Wypych 'PR' entry): 70-105 °C extrusion, 130 °C molding, 135-165 °C compression molding.

environmental.degradation_pathway: Enzymatic proteolysis (hydrolysis of peptide bonds) by proteases; readily biodegradable.
environmental.environmental_notes: Soy protein-based industrial material (Wypych 'PR' entry) shows low aquatic toxicity: Daphnia magna and rainbow trout 48 h LC50 both >1,000 mg/l.

carcinogenic_classification.value: not listed by ACGIH, NIOSH, NTP
